review_basis: Direct visual review of original WebP slides 29–33, including S3 PII findings, Config compliance branches, change-timeline timestamps, Inspector coverage and remediations.
part_title: Macie Sensitive-Data Discovery, AWS Config and Inspector Vulnerabilities

scenes.title: Amazon Macie
scenes.visual_overview: How Macie searches S3 objects for sensitive data, produces findings and supports review and remediation.
visual_walkthrough: S3 documents/logs/backup buckets
Macie ML and pattern matching
Finding with object, type, count, severity
EventBridge notification or optional automated response
Owner verifies finding, blocks exposure or removes unnecessary data
Bottom PII record and fictional SSN example
scenes.visual_example: A records.csv file includes a customer's name, email and a Social Security number; Macie identifies possible PII and generates a finding.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Sensitive-data discovery and notification are not automatic redaction or guaranteed prevention of leaks.
scenes.narration: This slide explains what Amazon Macie does with sensitive information stored in S3. The whole workflow answers a practical question: how do you find a personal identifier that may have been placed in the wrong object? Start at the S3 bucket group on the left, containing documents, logs and backups. The next purple panel shows Macie assessing supported S3 objects using machine-learning techniques and pattern matching. The arrow leads to a finding that identifies what was detected, the object's location, associated details and a severity assessment. Continue to EventBridge: findings can be routed to notifications or a configured response workflow, but generating a finding does not automatically delete or mask the data. The final owner panel shows human investigation: verify the result, restrict access by policy or block public access, and remediate unnecessary exposure. The worked example at the bottom is a customer-record CSV containing a name, email and fictional Social Security number. Macie raises a possible PII finding for the object. The team must decide whether the record is permitted and securely stored. Macie helps discover sensitive S3 data; it is different from Inspector's software vulnerability scans or Config's resource-setting checks.

scenes.title: AWS Config
scenes.visual_overview: How Config records resource configuration states, tests them against rules and shows compliance over time.
visual_walkthrough: S3, EC2, RDS feed configuration snapshots into AWS Config
AWS-managed and custom Config rules
Green compliant versus red noncompliant branch
History, SNS alert and investigation panel
Bottom public S3 bucket and SSH open 0.0.0.0/0 examples
CloudTrail actor versus Config resource-state comparison
scenes.visual_example: A Config rule flags a bucket configured for public read and another rule flags an EC2 security group with SSH open to every IP.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Config tells you what the recorded resource state is and whether a rule is met; CloudTrail can help identify the actor.
scenes.narration: This visual describes AWS Config as a history and rule-evaluation service for supported AWS resource settings. Begin with the left column of S3 buckets, EC2 instances, RDS databases and other resources. Configuration snapshots and changes are recorded by Config in the center. The next arrow leads to Config Rules. Managed rules supply predefined checks, while custom rules evaluate your own requirements. A resource follows a green compliant branch when it satisfies a rule, or a red noncompliant branch when it does not. On the right, the system can show compliance history and send configured notifications for someone to investigate. Look at the two bottom examples. A bucket with public access enabled fails a rule designed to prohibit public reads; a security group permitting SSH port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 fails a restricted-SSH rule. In both cases the service identifies a configuration condition; it does not guarantee it will remove it automatically. The comparison panel is important: AWS Config records the resulting resource state and its history, while CloudTrail records supported API calls and can help establish who changed it. The overall picture links resource inventory, policy evaluation and actionable follow-up.

scenes.title: Config Timeline: Resource State
scenes.visual_overview: How to correlate a configuration-state change in Config with a CloudTrail event identifying who made it.
visual_walkthrough: User or role calls PutBucketPolicy
Config detects and records new S3 bucket state
Resource timeline compares T1 before versus T2 after
CloudTrail lookup matches T2 event name, user identity, source IP
Bottom concrete timestamps and Alice example
scenes.visual_example: The bucket my-bucket has state before T1 13:20:01 and after T2 14:05:12; CloudTrail PutBucketPolicy at T2 is attributed to IAM user alice.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Combine state history with API event identity; neither service alone supplies the full who-and-what story.
scenes.narration: This diagram solves a very specific troubleshooting problem: a bucket policy changed, and you need to know what changed and who did it. Follow the four numbered steps. A user or role performs an API operation against Amazon S3, shown by the PutBucketPolicy call. AWS Config captures the resulting configuration state, and its resource timeline shows the previous state at time T1 and the new state at T2. That tells you what the setting looked like, but not necessarily which human performed the action. The fourth arrow leads to CloudTrail. Search a matching timestamp and API action to find the recorded userIdentity and source IP. The concrete example below uses my-bucket: the earlier state is shown at 13:20:01 and the updated policy at 14:05:12 on June tenth. A CloudTrail entry for PutBucketPolicy at the latter time names a user called Alice and shows a sample source IP. These are illustrative audit fields; the relevant CloudTrail event must actually have been recorded and retained. Read the exam cue as a division of labor: Config explains configuration history, while CloudTrail supports actor attribution. Together they make an auditable investigation possible.

scenes.title: Amazon Inspector
scenes.visual_overview: How Inspector assesses supported compute workloads for vulnerable software and unintended network exposure.
visual_walkthrough: Left EC2 instances, ECR container images and Lambda function coverage
Center assessments of packages, code and EC2 network exposure
Findings severity Critical/High/Medium/Low
Right distinction from Macie's S3 sensitive-data discovery
Bottom vulnerable public EC2 web application, patch and network restriction example
scenes.visual_example: Inspector identifies a critical vulnerable package on a publicly reachable EC2 web server; engineers update the package and limit exposure.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A prioritized finding guides human remediation, not automatic patching or a universal scan of every resource.
scenes.narration: This slide introduces Amazon Inspector as a vulnerability-assessment service, not a general-purpose data classifier. The left panel lists its supported workload types: EC2 instances, container images in Amazon ECR and Lambda function code or dependencies where supported. Trace their arrows into Inspector in the middle. It assesses relevant software vulnerabilities, and for EC2 also examines unintended network exposure. The output is a findings list with severity levels such as Critical, High, Medium and Low so the team can prioritize work. Notice the comparison panel on the right. Macie looks for personal or otherwise sensitive information in S3 objects; Inspector looks for software or exposure risks in workloads. The bottom story makes the difference concrete. An EC2 instance runs a public web app. Inspector reports a critical vulnerable installed package and a potentially reachable service. The remediation step is to investigate, update the affected package or deployment, and restrict network access as appropriate. Then reassess the resource to confirm the issue is resolved. Inspection does not automatically secure a resource, and coverage depends on the workload and supported scan type. The complete picture is discover, assess, prioritize, fix and verify.

scenes.title: Inspector Coverage and Vulnerability Assessment
scenes.visual_overview: A detailed Inspector pipeline connects EC2, ECR and Lambda resource assessment to severity-based remediation.
visual_walkthrough: Workload boxes: EC2 packages/network, ECR image OS/dependencies, Lambda code
Inspector discovers, analyzes and correlates supported findings
Severity column Critical/High/Medium/Low/Informational
Right action steps investigate, prioritize, patch/rebuild/redeploy, reassess
Bottom end-to-end example across three workload types
scenes.visual_example: An EC2 instance, ECR image and Lambda function each produce supported findings, which lead to package updates, rebuilt images or code changes.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Inspector findings require a remediation cycle; severity alone does not prove exploitability or perform a fix.
scenes.narration: This is a closer walkthrough of Inspector's coverage and what an engineer should do after a scan. Across the left are three distinct asset types. EC2 assessments look at installed packages and supported network reachability signals. ECR scans container images, including relevant operating system and language dependencies. Lambda scanning examines supported function code or dependencies. Follow those arrows into Inspector's central panel: it discovers eligible resources, analyzes vulnerabilities, correlates relevant exposure where supported, and continues reassessing new or changed workloads. The next column lists finding severity from Critical through High, Medium, Low and Informational. These labels help prioritize investigation; they do not replace review of business impact, reachability or available fixes. Now trace the right-side remediation staircase. First review the affected resource and evidence, then prioritize, update vulnerable packages or rebuild an image or function, redeploy, and reassess. The bottom example shows EC2, ECR and Lambda feeding findings and a final remediation action. The exam cue contrasts supported workload types and emphasizes that EC2 network reachability is an Inspector capability. The overarching lesson is that vulnerability management is a repeatable detect, correct and verify loop rather than a single scan.
